title: By welcoming Deion Sanders, the Browns show they've learned their lesson from last season Deion Sanders finally had his moment with Browns' coach and GM. Hopefully, the team will convince Shedeur Sanders supporters all is well. Jason Lloyd 18

BEREA, Ohio — The biggest lesson the Cleveland Browns learned from last season had nothing to do with on-field performance and everything to do with off-field performance.

full_text:
Deion Sanders takes a good look at his son, Browns quarterback Shedeur Sanders, at the conclusion of the second day of training camp. Andrew Dolph / USA Today via Reuters Connect
BEREA, Ohio — The biggest lesson the Cleveland Browns learned from last season had nothing to do with on-field performance and everything to do with off-field performance.
The Browns never properly bent the knee to Deion Sanders and his legion of fans last year after selecting Shedeur Sanders in the NFL Draft. They have spent the past seven months trying to rectify that oversight.
Shortly after Todd Monken was introduced as head coach in January, one of the first orders of business was rushing out a social media clip of Monken welcoming Shedeur into his office and telling him how much he likes him. That was no coincidence after so many silly conspiracy theories about “sabotage” emerged last season.
The Browns took the next necessary step Thursday when they welcomed Deion to practice with wide smiles and outstretched arms.
the Sanders duo🤩 pic.twitter.com/psLbgf9hLR
— Cleveland Browns (@Browns) July 30, 2026
“That was really cool. That was Deion Sanders, are you kidding me?” Monken said Thursday after meeting with Coach Prime. “Forget that it’s Shedeur’s dad. First of all, he did an unbelievable job with Shedeur — great kid, obviously an elite football player, baseball player. And then as a coach, I mean, everything he’s achieved, that was awesome.”
Shedeur told his father to stay away from camp last year because he wanted to be in a better situation when Dad showed up. So Monken and general manager Andrew Berry spent time with Deion before the Browns taking the field Thursday in part because Deion made it clear he wanted to meet with them, so he could tell them more about Shedeur.
“I want to meet (Monken) because I think it’s vital that as a coach, not the dad, I can tell him a few things about (Shedeur), how to get him going,” Sanders said during his appearance earlier this year on “The Barbershop” podcast with Garrett Bush . “That wasn’t asked of me a year ago. I don’t understand it.”
Sanders clearly is an excellent father and has done a good job raising all of his sons. He’s also used to getting what he wants. It’s hard to separate father from college coach in this instance, and there’s an argument to be made that neither belongs in an NFL facility advising the head coach.
I don’t recall Oregon’s Dan Lanning visiting Cleveland to talk about Dillon Gabriel or Sam Pittman or Bobby Petrino flying in to talk to Monken about Taylen Green. Nevertheless, there are unique rules of engagement when it comes to the Sanders family. The Browns learned that the hard way last season.
Deion Sanders finally had his moment with the head coach and general manager. Hopefully, the Browns have done enough to convince the Sanders’ rabid, loyal fan base and vocal Sanders family supporters like Cam Newton , Robert Griffin III and any other former players who spoke out against Shedeur Sanders’ “mistreatment” last year that all is starting anew. Monken appears to have dodged the sabotage allegations for now, although that could change once he names a starter.
The reality is Sanders had a lot to learn about playing quarterback in the NFL last year and is now getting the opportunity to show all that he worked on. There are more weapons on this offense compared to last year. The offensive line has new faces, although the level of improvement is still to be determined.
There are no more excuses. It’s on Sanders to perform. Given what else the Browns have at quarterback, he will eventually get his chance.
I’m on record that if forced to choose between Sanders and Deshaun Watson, I’ll take Sanders every time. Monken and the Browns may not see it that way. Through the first couple of days of training camp, I’m not sure Watson is still capable of playing quarterback in the NFL, but the Browns are going to give him every opportunity to win this job out of camp. If Watson manages to beat out Sanders, it will tell you without telling you what the Browns think of Sanders’ NFL future.
It is widely presumed the Browns will be back hunting quarterbacks in the 2027 draft, although Shedeur will eventually get the runway to change that. This is Cleveland, where multiple quarterbacks have started games in 24 of 27 seasons since 1999. At least three quarterbacks have started games in four of the last five years.
Deion quietly watched practice Thursday from high atop the bleachers. With no fans in attendance, Sanders could roam freely without being bothered. He met with Shedeur briefly afterward while cameras buzzed around them.
During their brief time together, Monken said he mostly talked NIL, Jackson State and Colorado with Deion. Monken, of course, served as offensive coordinator at Georgia and understands the state of the college game.
“We really didn’t get into almost any football,” Monken said.
In that case, this may not have been the last of Deion in Cleveland.

full_text:
Can rookie Red Murdock go from Mr. Irrelevant to a key piece of the Broncos' linebacker group? David Zalubowski / Associated Press
The Denver Broncos officially open training camp Friday after two days of condensed “acclimation” workouts earlier in the week. It marks the start of Denver’s chase for the franchise’s fourth Super Bowl title and first since the 2015 season, but in a micro sense it also lights the fuse on some intriguing position battles that could help shape the roster when it takes an initial 53-man form in early September.
We don’t have to wait that long, though, to take a stab at how that Week 1 group could come together. Below is our second offseason roster projection. The final version will follow after the Broncos’ preseason finale against the Minnesota Vikings on Aug. 28.
It is possible the Broncos will keep three quarterbacks on their roster. They did it in 2024 when Zach Wilson served as the emergency No. 3 on game days. The Broncos have been pleased with Ehlinger’s growth during his second year in the offense, and head coach Sean Payton seemed to suggest during the annual NFL meeting in March that the 27-year-old could even compete for the backup job behind Nix. I still have a hard time seeing Payton moving on from Stidham, even after a couple of critical mistakes during his lone start in the AFC Championship Game in January. However, it also wouldn’t be a total shock to see Ehlinger steal that spot if he puts together an impressive camp and preseason.
J.K. Dobbins, RJ Harvey, Jonah Coleman
Others: Jaleel McLaughlin, Tyler Badie, Cody Schrader
The Broncos kept four running backs on cutdown day each of the past two seasons, but there were only three on Payton’s opening roster in 2023 (Javonte Williams, Samaje Perine, McLaughlin). Given that Harvey and Coleman are entering their second and first seasons, respectively, the Broncos may keep Badie or McLaughlin on the roster. But McLaughlin was a game-day inactive as the No. 4 back last season during all but one of the first 10 games, when all the running backs were healthy, so I think the Broncos will use that roster spot on a different position this time around.
The Broncos could release Prentice, a veteran who wouldn’t be subject to waivers, on cutdown day and then bring him back to the practice squad with a plan to elevate him on game day until a spot opens on the roster. It’s how they maneuvered last season with Prentice and in the past with former fullback Michael Burton. It’s also possible the Broncos don’t need to significantly finagle the roster and just put Prentice on the opening 53. Either way, Prentice will be the team’s fullback when the season begins.
Courtland Sutton, Jaylen Waddle, Marvin Mims, Troy Franklin, Pat Bryant
Others: Lil’Jordan Humphrey, Michael Bandy, Hakeem Butler, Dane Key, Joseph Manjack, Cameron Ross, Kolbe Katsis
The big question here is not who will make the roster, but rather who will emerge as the team’s No. 3 target behind Sutton and Waddle. Bryant, heading into his second season, had a strong spring and could benefit from the space Waddle can create in the passing game. A player to watch in the preseason: Butler, the former UFL standout who joined the team in June and presents a massive target at 6-foot-5 and 227 pounds.
Adam Trautman, Evan Engram, Justin Joly, Caleb Lohner
Others: Nate Adkins, Dallen Bentley, Lucas Krull
Lohner drew unsolicited praise from Payton during rookie minicamp in May, saying the 2025 seventh-round pick has made major strides related to his understanding of the game after playing only one season of college football. The 6-foot-7, 250-pound former basketball player could be a unique target in the red zone. He missed the Broncos’ acclimation practices this week while recovering from a lower-body injury, but Lohner figures to have a real shot to make the roster. Still, the depth spots at tight end could be among the most hotly contested on the roster.
Garett Bolles, Ben Powers, Luke Wattenberg, Quinn Meinerz, Mike McGlinchey, Alex Palczewski, Kage Casey, Alex Forsyth, Frank Crum, Matt Peart
Others: Nick Gargiulo, Reid Holskey, Gavin Ortega, Calvin Throckmorton, Michael Deiter, Tyler Miller
The offensive line benefited in this exercise by there being one less player in the running back room. Forsyth and Peart figure to be the bubble players for a group that added a fourth-round pick in Casey to a room that has largely been the same past three years. The Broncos may keep both, though, as insurance for a line that is among the league’s older and more experienced units.
Zach Allen, D.J. Jones, Malcolm Roach, Eyioma Uwazurike, Tyler Onyedim, Sai’vion Jones
Others: Jordan Jackson, Kristian Williams, Matt Henningsen, Jordan Miller
Jackson has been a veteran contributor for the Broncos the past two seasons, playing in 24 regular-season and playoff games, and it’s possible the Broncos could keep him as a seventh defensive lineman. Uwazurike saw his role increase for Denver last season and figures to be a prominent interior presence as he enters the final year of his rookie contract. A major question in this room is which young defensive end — Onyedim or Jones — pushes for early playing time as the fifth defensive lineman in the rotation.
Nik Bonitto, Jonathon Cooper, Jonah Elliss, Dondrea Tillman, Que Robinson
Others: Drew Sanders, Dasan McCullough, Johnny Walker
Will Cooper, who faces a second-degree felony charge with an arraignment date in late August, face a suspension from the NFL for violation of its personal conduct policy? For now, the Broncos are operating with Cooper being a member of the roster , but they could keep extra numbers in this room as they build contingencies for a possible extended absence for the veteran edge rusher. If he can stay healthy — a moving target during his first three seasons in the league — Sanders could be a depth answer for the Broncos on the edge.
Alex Singleton, Justin Strnad, Red Murdock, Karene Reid
Others: Jordan Turner, Levelle Bailey, Taurean York
Confidence level in the depth chart rankings beyond Singleton and Strnad: low. The Broncos have a room full of intriguing, but largely unproven linebackers behind the two veteran starters. Several of them could be asked to play significant roles at some point this season. The battles to find out who those players will be qualify as some of the most intriguing ones we’ll see in this camp.
Pat Surtain, Riley Moss, Ja’Quan McMillian, Kris Abrams-Draine , Jahdae Barron
Others: Sean Fresch Jr., Brent Austin, Reese Taylor, Jaden Robinson, Sam Webb
The top five here are all but set, but it will be interesting to see whether Fresch, a former UFL standout with return potential who was signed in the spring, can put together a strong case to be added as a sixth corner. His end zone interception Thursday in front of Katsis during a red-zone period was arguably the top play made during Denver’s two acclimation practices.
Talanoa Hufanga, Brandon Jones, Devon Key, JL Skinner, Tycen Anderson
Others: Miles Scott, Parker Robertson
Scott, the seventh-round pick out of Illinois, could certainly play his way into a Week 1 roster spot. With P.J. Locke now with the Dallas Cowboys, the Broncos need a reliable No. 3 safety. Key has the most experience in that position among the reserves on this expanded roster, but the Broncos will give Scott plenty of opportunity in camp. Ultimately, though, we went with a pair of potential impact special teams players in Skinner and Anderson to round out this group.
Wil Lutz (kicker), Jeremy Crawshaw (punter), Mitchell Fraboni (long snapper)
Other: Luke Basso (long snapper)
Crawshaw’s punts so far this offseason have been things of sky-scraping beauty. On the heels of an excellent performance in the playoffs, the punter could be a major weapon for the Broncos in his second season.

full_text:
Dolphins coach Jeff Hafley could struggle to win games in Year 1 with some much of the team's cap space tied up in players no longer with the team. Megan Briggs / Getty Images
MIAMI GARDENS, Fla. — Ghosts of the Miami Dolphins’ past hovered Wednesday, as the team’s latest incarnation conducted its opening practice of training camp at the Baptist Health Training Complex.
While there’s no doubt reason for excitement about this new era under first-year general manager Jon-Eric Sullivan and first-year coach Jeff Hafley — the tandem of former Green Bay Packers who have been chosen to lead an unprecedented rebuild in Miami — they also recognize that to reach the fortunes of a better future, the Dolphins must become unshackled by the errors of their all-too-recent past.
And that’s going to take time. And money.
The Dolphins’ $179.2 million in dead salary cap is the most in NFL history, and they’re at a distinct financial disadvantage with their books clogged by players who currently ply their trade elsewhere, if anywhere at all. With roughly $120 million in cap space projected to their top-53 players, according to Over The Cap, the Dolphins are essentially rostering a team under the salary cap constraints of the 2011 season — a time when Tom Brady and Peyton Manning paced the quarterback market with contracts worth $18 million annually.
The Dolphins are realistic about their timeline, and they were willing to let the accounting department (and ownership) take one on the chin in the short term. Even so, there was a clear method behind the mayhem.
Tua Tagovailoa became the first $50 million quarterback to lose his job for performance. Tagovailoa, who accounts for $55.4 million in dead money in 2026, was a necessary cut to symbolize a new era. From there, the Dolphins released wide receiver Tyreek Hill ($28.2 million in dead money), linebacker Bradley Chubb ($11 million) and traded wideout Jaylen Waddle ($23.2 million) for a first-round pick and safety Minkah Fitzpatrick ($13 million) in a cap dump.
Since the 2025 trade of Jalen Ramsey ($20.8 million) and the retirement of tackle Terron Armstead ($10.7 million) are still on the books, seven of the Dolphins’ nine biggest cap hits currently belong to players who won’t play a snap for them this season.
To put it another way, the Dolphins’ $179.2 million in dead cap space would equate to the fifth-most expensive unit in the NFL.
Sullivan knew what he was getting into when he took the job, however, and he and the Dolphins were decisive. Rather than slow-playing the teardown to spread out the financial burden, the Dolphins jettisoned every remaining highly paid star from the previous regime. They are willingly taking on an historic cap beating in 2026 and will still be forced to navigate around $56.7 million in dead money in 2027. Beyond that, they’re unburdened.
If Sullivan and Hafley can develop their deep 2026 draft class in the meantime, the Dolphins could have a new core in place and a clean slate with the books.
In the much shorter term, the Dolphins have focused on culture. And with 40 players signed to one-year contracts, the Dolphins are stocked with guys who have something to prove.
That suits their overall purpose just fine.
“We brought in a lot of culture guys who we feel are wired right for what we're trying to build,” Sullivan told The Athletic this week. “It's a starting point. I like the culture we have, and that's a testament to the guys we brought in, both your rookies, as well as some of the vets who are on one-years and some of the guys who were already here.
“I think (Hafley) has done an incredible job of being very upfront and messaging the team in terms of what we're going to be about, which is mental resilience, physical resilience, work ethic, toughness. I've said it a million times over again. We're going to move a certain way here, and we're going to weed out the guys who don't belong.”
They’ll have to be a blue-collar team because, relatively speaking, that’s who they are. Defensive lineman Zach Sieler ($11.4 million) and linebacker Jordyn Brooks ($10.9 million) own the largest cap hits on the team. Miami doesn't have another player on the roster with a cap hit north of $7 million.
There are 316 active players in the NFL — an average of about 10 per team — with a cap hit of at least $7 million, according to Spotrac. Seiler and Brooks rank 172nd and 180th in the NFL, respectively. The Dolphins are truly a team in cap jail.
To break it down further, the Dolphins predictably rank last in both offensive and defensive cap investments, but the disparity between their peers is alarming, according to Spotrac.
They’ve got $61.9 million in offensive cap spending, while the New York Jets rank No. 31 with $96 million; the Cleveland Browns are 30th with $116.1 million. Nearly every team in the league has spent at least twice the cap space on offensive players, while the Rams, Bucs and Cowboys have tripled the Dolphins’ offensive cap spending.
Defensively, the Dolphins’ $57.6 million in cap spending trails the 31st-ranked Philadelphia Eagles by $10.7 million, while 18 teams have spent at least twice as much. The Pittsburgh Steelers ($163.6 million) tripled the Dolphins’ defensive cap spending.
Keep in mind, the Dolphins have just $11.7 million in cap space, so they’re doing what they can.
Unsurprisingly, the Dolphins are also ranked near the bottom of cap spending at the premium positions. They’re 30th at quarterback ($8.5 million), where Malik Willis is a full-time starter for the first time. They rank last at wide receiver ($13.2 million), 31st on the offensive line ($31.2 million) and the edge ($12.2 million) and 30th at cornerback ($15.4 million).
Sullivan and Hafley will focus on the foundation, both on the field and in the financials. They’ll continue to be deliberate, an approach that’s well-ingrained in Sullivan after 22 years with the Packers.
And they’ll work to try to ensure this historic bout with dead money was worth the unprecedented challenge.

title: If Harrison Smith doesn't return to the Vikings, the defense will need a new leader Smith has made the Vikings defense special. Will he back for a 15th season, or does Brian Flores need to find a new leader on the back end? Alec Lewis 2
summary:
Safety Harrison Smith has played 14 seasons for the Vikings and is the active leader with 39 career interceptions. Stephen Maturen / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — One of the secrets to the recent success of the Minnesota Vikings defense doesn’t show up in the numbers.
You can find how many coverages they deploy to deceive. You can check blitz rates. But unless you’re really looking for it, unless you’re paying intense attention to all 11 defenders before the snap, you will miss the communication.
full_text:
Safety Harrison Smith has played 14 seasons for the Vikings and is the active leader with 39 career interceptions. Stephen Maturen / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — One of the secrets to the recent success of the Minnesota Vikings defense doesn’t show up in the numbers.
You can find how many coverages they deploy to deceive. You can check blitz rates. But unless you’re really looking for it, unless you’re paying intense attention to all 11 defenders before the snap, you will miss the communication.
Minnesota’s secondary often plays like it’s connected by a string. Players move in tandem. They replace each other in spots. Their synergy seems unbothered by the noise, the setting or the opponent. The Vikings defense takes pride in its ability to change plans on the fly, depending on what it sees from the offense.
“Getting a chance to play last year,” safety Jay Ward said, “I was happy. But for our defense’s standard, I had to uphold the role of not messing up or busting plays. Because we haven’t been doing that.”
The Vikings defense’s blowing a coverage happened so rarely that seeing it during last summer’s joint practices with the New England Patriots felt like spotting an eclipse. It was jarring. One reason it occurred was the absence of one of the core players who has operated the defense’s controls: potential Hall of Fame safety Harrison Smith.
As with every efficient operation, the Vikings’ connectivity hinged on the people. Remove the man who has lived and learned from more than 13,000 snaps, and you are eliminating perhaps the most important link in the chain.
This brings us to the present. Smith, 37, remains undecided about whether to return for a 15th NFL season. The Vikings don’t expect a resolution in the short term. And Smith, who has stayed in shape this offseason, prefers to feel fully convinced about his decision when the time arrives. Already this week, some of Smith’s former coaches and teammates have lobbied for his return.
Defensive coordinator Brian Flores chuckled at himself after calling Smith “absent.”
“I still haven’t gotten over it,” he said. “I love him dearly. I hope he hears that. He knows what I mean by that.”
Linebacker Blake Cashman added, “Hitman is always welcome here. He’s not going to give anybody a definitive answer, but he’s earned the right to take as much time as he needs.”
While waiting for a decision, the Vikings know they cannot afford to take his void for granted. Veteran safety Josh Metellus said not having Smith was like missing a major portion of the pie chart that allows Minnesota’s defense to stay amorphous and problematic. For that reason, the unit spent most of the spring’s organized team activities toggling through possibilities.
Metellus and fellow safety Theo Jackson orchestrated some of the operation. Rookie third-round pick Jakobe Thomas took a turn. Because Cashman missed the spring rehabbing a finger injury, fellow linebackers Eric Wilson and Ivan Pace Jr. took turns with the responsibilities.
It came in the form of hand signals and verbal communication from all areas of the field. Imagine the picture: quarterback positioned under center, a receiver going in motion from one side of the line of scrimmage to the other, the defense countering the changing offensive picture in real time.
In 2025, NFL offenses used motion on 62.3 percent of the snaps, according to Next Gen Stats. Most of those movements happen with a purpose. So, the onus falls on the defense to not only respond but also to predict the offense’s intent. This requires thinking, understanding and reacting.
Having that ability in previous seasons — often in the form of Smith — is what made the Vikings’ defensive secret a secret.
“There’s nothing that’s not communicated,” Metellus said. “As a safety, naturally, you wouldn’t not check with your counterparts to make sure you’re on the same page. We never really go without checking with the guys we’re playing with. We’ve built that.”
Metellus’ capacity for on-field adjustments intrigued the Vikings years ago. It’s one of the primary features of his positional versatility. To line up in numerous places, you have to know where to start before the snap and where to end up after the snap. Last fall, the Vikings trusted his knowledge of the system enough to allow him to call a series of plays in the preseason.
Because he frequently plays in the slot, he can quickly pass messages to Cashman on the second level. Finalizing a vocal liaison on the third level will be a priority throughout training camp. Ward highlighted the smarts of third-round rookie Jakobe Thomas and undrafted free agent Jacob Thomas. Jackson, who played 530 defensive snaps last year, is another viable option.
Until Smith makes his decision, this element of the defense will warrant attention. Communication is only as good as those doing the communicating.
• The Vikings’ starting edge rushers are solidified. Andrew Van Ginkel will play his prototypical role, which allows him to extend off the ball and in coverage. Meanwhile, third-year man Dallas Turner will assume the pass-rush-heavy spot on the line of scrimmage that Jonathan Greenard had occupied.
The depth is still a question mark. Behind those two, the best option might be Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins. The 2025 fifth-round pick mixed in to give the starters a breather Thursday.
His overall development as he transitions to edge rusher is an underrated feature of the roster. That said, it shouldn’t preclude Minnesota from adding another veteran who could fill in, in the event of an injury.
• Second-year receiver Myles Price made multiple catches the first two days of training camp, including an impressive adjustment Thursday on a Carson Wentz deep ball. Price, the team’s primary return man, played seven offensive snaps down the stretch of the 2025 season.
Considering the Vikings might infuse their system with new wrinkles featuring motion and misdirection, Price’s continued improvement could provide another offensive asset.

full_text:
DeVonta Smith leads the way for Philadelphia Eagles wide receivers in 2026. Terence Lewis / Icon Sportswire via Getty Images
There’s one month to go until the Philadelphia Eagles’ 90-man roster must be pared to 53 on Aug. 30. Between now and then, the coaches have four weeks of practices and three preseason games to evaluate.
After two practice sessions and a glimpse at the early-summer depth chart, The Athletic ’s Zach Berman and Brooks Kubena offer their first 53-man roster projections. Look for more projections as training camp and the preseason continue throughout August.
Kubena (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Andy Dalton
After watching two days of Cole Payton, I do not think the Eagles can afford to trade McKee in training camp — unless they acquire another reliable veteran. It is early, but so far, Payton is living down to the weaknesses in his scouting report. He threw three interceptions in Thursday’s practice. He is off target, unbalanced and indecisive. The Eagles could sign him to the practice squad to develop more.
Berman (3): Jalen Hurts, Tanner McKee, Cole Payton
I see a realistic pathway for Payton to make the roster because my guess is the Eagles will trade Tanner McKee or Andy Dalton. It doesn’t make sense to keep three veterans. There are too many teams that could use a backup quarterback, and my guess is Dalton will have trade value next month.
Kubena (4): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley, Dameon Pierce
Bigsby’s gashing touchdown run in Thursday’s practice provided more evidence he can be an explosive complement to Barkley. I would be surprised if any other back gets more than 30 touches this season. But Shipley’s pass-catching ability makes him a good fit in an emergency, and Elijah Mitchell thrived in this system during his rookie year in San Francisco. Pierce might not be a fit. He had early success with the Houston Texans, but his touches diminished over the years as the franchise shifted toward more zone concepts. Sean Mannion could leverage Pierce’s 5-foot-10, 215-pound build to create the H-back looks not filled by his tight ends.
Berman (3): Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, Will Shipley
Watch out for Bigsby as a contributing player for the Eagles — not just a Barkley insurance plan — and Shipley will be the No. 3 running back and a contributing player on special teams. I like Pierce and Mitchell, but a fourth running back might be a luxury and better as an early-season practice squad option.
Kubena (6): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Hollywood Brown, Elijah Moore, Makai Lemon, Johnny Wilson
I expect the Eagles to roster more wide receivers this year. Part of that is mathematical. Smith and A.J. Brown combined for 234 targets last year, and the former is the only receiver remaining whose present capacity warrants more than 100 targets. Roseman also views this unit as a “basketball squad.” Some of their roles are unique. Many are interchangeable. Wilson’s 6-6, 228-pound frame makes him a tough cut because he is a difficult matchup and adds blocking in the run game.
Berman (5): DeVonta Smith, Dontayvion Wicks, Makai Lemon, Hollywood Brown, Johnny Wilson
I don’t see the Eagles going deep here for the sake of it. I wanted to keep Darius Cooper, but that “dirty work” receiver could come down to Cooper vs. Wilson. This will be a summer competition. Elijah Moore is intriguing, although my guess is Brown or Moore for one roster spot. Perhaps the Eagles will go deeper — Brooks’ reasoning is sound — but I have them going with more numbers at tight end and on the offensive line.
Kubena (3): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers
Goedert still represents this room’s most dangerous target — so long as the 31-year-old remains healthy. The Eagles spent a second-round pick on Goedert’s presumed successor, Stowers, who is a proficient pass-catcher but still needs to adjust to blocking NFL-caliber defenders. That latter half is what Mundt is for. Grant Calcaterra struggled as a blocker last season, and the one-year, $2 million contract he signed in the offseason offers little to no security. I would expect to see Jenkins and Latu on the practice squad again.
Berman: (4): Dallas Goedert, Johnny Mundt, Eli Stowers, Cameron Latu
I think the Eagles will roster a “fullback” in their new offense, and Latu makes sense as a fullback/tight end/special teams hybrid. Otherwise, same logic as Brooks — Goedert is the top tight end, Stowers is the pass-catching reserve, and Mundt is the blocking reserve.
Kubena (9): Lane Johnson, Jordan Mailata, Markel Bell, Fred Johnson, Cam Jurgens, Landon Dickerson, Tyler Steen, Myles Hinton, Drew Kendall
The swing tackle battle is still in … full swing between Bell and Fred Johnson. But given Philadelphia’s third-round investment in Bell, the odds are stacked against Fred Johnson. Hinton, a sixth-round pick in 2025, continues to see reps at second-team left guard. Kendall is getting second-team reps at guard, too. I have not seen Kendall take snaps at center yet in training camp, but the Eagles know from his days at Boston College he can play the position.
Berman (10): Jordan Mailata, Landon Dickerson, Cam Jurgens, Tyler Steen, Lane Johnson, Fred Johnson, Markel Bell, Drew Kendall, Myles Hinton, Micah Morris
I have the Eagles going deeper on the offensive line to develop their young linemen. Morris, a sixth-round pick who plays on the interior, makes sense to keep. Cameron Williams left practice early Thursday; it’ll be interesting to monitor his status. I was debating between Williams and Hinton before the injury and leaned toward Hinton because of position flexibility. Perhaps the Eagles will keep Michael Jordan because of his starting experience. What about Willie Lampkin, a player who intrigued the front office when it claimed him off waivers last summer?
Kubena (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Gabe Hall, Byron Young, Ty Robinson
Nothing will have changed on the defensive line — and that’s a good thing for the Eagles. Bernard is still very raw in training camp. Fangio said Uar Bernard is on the “P.P.” plan: “Patience and persistence.” The Eagles will have to waive Bernard because of the seventh-round pick’s draft status, but it would be somewhat surprising to see another team try to poach a player who just put shoulder pads on for the first time. The Eagles are invested in developing Bernard, and the NFL allows teams a 17th practice-squad player if they are part of the International Player Pathway program.
Berman (6): Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis, Moro Ojomo, Byron Young, Ty Robinson, Uar Bernard
Perhaps Bernard might suffer an injury in the summer that would allow the Eagles to stash him on injured reserve. Short of IR, I’ll project him for the initial 53-man roster with the Eagles committed to his development. They could put him on the practice squad as an international player, although I’m curious whether another team would claim him off waivers and keep him on its 53-man roster and build its own development plan.
Kubena (5): Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie, A.J. Epenesa
The Eagles do not expect Greenard’s pectoral strain to be a long-term injury. Greenard’s Week 1 start remains a goal. Fangio said he will “miss a good bit of camp.” If it’s a longer recovery, the Eagles can use Greenard’s roster spot for someone else by keeping Greenard on the physically unable to perform list entering the regular season. But then, Greenard must miss at least four games. Ebiketie, who totaled 16.5 sacks in four seasons with the Atlanta Falcons, is consistently second in the rotation in training camp. Fangio has been complimentary of Epenesa, who intercepted Payton in Thursday’s practice.
Berman (5): Jonathan Greenard, Jalyx Hunt, Nolan Smith, Arnold Ebiketie, A.J. Epenesa
No disagreements here. The wild card to watch is Brandon Graham. If the Eagles bring Graham back for a 17th season — and he’s expressed an interest in participating in training camp — they’ll either go deeper…

full_text:
The Commanders are getting after it in training camp. Scott Taetsch / Getty Images
ASHBURN, Va. — By the time cornerback Rasul Douglas ended Thursday morning’s practice session for the Washington Commanders with an interception that had defensive players hooting and hollering, Washington’s offense had long settled into an early training camp lull. The second day of Commanders training camp was marked by a slew of dropped passes spread over multiple receivers and backs — and a dominant, disruptive performance by the defense.
“They had a really good day,” top wide receiver Terry McLaurin said. “I’m not afraid to say that.”
Two days of workouts don’t make a season — or even a training camp. The Commanders won’t so much as put on pads until next week. But these practices are scrutinized by coaches and players alike.
“You want to ask: ‘What was the intent of the play? Did we make the right check? Did we go to the right location?’” coach Dan Quinn said. “That could be at any number of spots. You want to evaluate what specific things you want to nail for tomorrow.”
Which is a longer way of saying: What happens on the practice field matters each day. After two workouts — and with only a walkthrough scheduled for Friday — here’s what stood out for the Commanders.
No topic has taken up more air time and ink in Washington’s offseason than whether the team has enough talent and depth at receiver. When camp opened Wednesday, Treylon Burks — a former first-round pick with Tennessee who caught 10 passes for 130 yards in eight games with the Commanders in 2025 — spent much of his time with the first team.
Burks, though, sat out Thursday’s practice with what Quinn described as soreness in his foot.
“Something that we’re not looking at as a long-term one,” Quinn said.
Still, with McLaurin the only receiver likely to scare opposing defenses, each practice is an opportunity for the remaining players to make plays. Burks’ injury may indeed be minor, and it’s possible he could be back on the field as soon as Saturday.
But his absence Thursday again raises questions about his durability — questions that have dogged him since his rookie year of 2022. Burks, 26, has never played in more than 11 games in a season and has never had more targets (54), catches (33) or yards (444) than he did as a rookie.
With Burks out, third-year receiver Luke McCaffrey and veteran free-agent signee Van Jefferson spent most of the time alongside McLaurin in three-receiver sets. Tight end Chig Okonkwo is also versatile enough to line up on the outside.
Quarterback Jayden Daniels — the linchpin of this entire operation — had an uneven first day of camp, throwing behind several receivers during a session focused exclusively on red zone play.
“You’re gonna have good days, you’re gonna have bad days,” Daniels said. “It’s part of football. It’s part of camp. … I’d rather fail in camp than come the season. You try to be critical. You take the coaching.”
One part of that coaching this offseason has been the use of cameras attached to the quarterbacks’ helmets that can be used for film study after practice. While Daniels cautions that the tape doesn’t always provide what the quarterback sees — “My eyes might be somewhere else, but my helmet’s that way,” he said — the coaching staff has learned that it can evaluate how quarterbacks are communicating the calls in the huddle and at the line of scrimmage.
“You want to listen to it,” Daniels said, “listen to how you call the play, how you’re calling the play and make sure you’re delivering a message, painting a picture to the other guys in the huddle to understand the play.”
When the Commanders cut veteran center Tyler Biadasz in February, it left Nick Allegretti — who has spent all but a handful of snaps during a seven-year career at guard — as the starting center.
“I love center,” Allegretti, who is still listed as a guard on the Commanders’ roster, said during offseason workouts. “I love the mental side of the game. It’s a challenging place to play. It’s mentally demanding, making important calls and protection adjustments at the line of scrimmage.”
Allegretti, though, suffered a calf injury in Wednesday’s first workout and therefore sat out Thursday. Quinn said the injury is unlikely to hold Allegretti out for long, but it immediately put a spotlight on Julian Good-Jones, a 29-year-old veteran who has appeared in one NFL game, and rookie Matt Gulbin, a sixth-round pick out of Michigan State in this year’s NFL Draft.
Good-Jones, whose lone appearance came in 2023 with Washington, took first-team snaps Thursday. He has spent much of the past three seasons on the Commanders’ practice squad.
“Dude, it’s a blast,” Good-Jones said Thursday. “I’ve been here a while now, and these are my guys. This is what we prepare for. I’ve been lucky enough that here, we mix guys up all the time. So I feel comfortable playing next to whoever they put me with.”
Thursday brought the first live kicking competition of camp, with veteran Jake Moody and rookie Drew Stevens each getting the chance to kick six field goals in rapid succession and then kicking again after what would have been “fourth down” in 11-on-11 drills.
Moody, a former third-round pick of San Francisco, made all six of his attempts from distances that gradually worked their way back to perhaps 50 yards. (Note: the kicking competition was held on a low field, and reporters couldn’t get a vantage point that allowed them to see the yard lines.) He then made two more following 11-on-11 situations.
Stevens, an undrafted free agent from Iowa with an extremely strong leg, also nailed each of his six attempts and then made his only kick following 11-on-11 play. Stevens made 76 of 95 field goals and 124 of 126 extra points in a four-year career at Iowa.
The Commanders have used seven different kickers in the three years of general manager Adam Peters’ tenure.
During the periods of practice when the offense faces the defense — either in 11-on-11 or skeleton drills without the offensive and defensive lines — the defensive players and coaches stand on one side of the field, with their offensive counterparts on the opposite sideline.
That leaves Quinn as the lone exception. He spent the first two days of practice watching from various points close to the action — including from the center’s position when the linemen weren’t on the field. This positioning isn’t an accident.
“Sometimes I want to see the eyes of the defense, if it’s zone, to see where they’re looking,” Quinn said. “If they have vision of the quarterback, I want to make sure I am seeing where their eyes are. …
“Sometimes I want to see it from the offensive perspective to where I’m the center, I’m the quarterback, I’m seeing spacing, I’m seeing timing. And that’s really where I can also see the accuracy, like balls thrown on the right side in a zone to extend plays. Just small cues that I’m trying to find that I may have not seen from a sideline perspective.”
After Friday’s walk-through — closed to fans and media — the Commanders will welcome fans to practice for the first time on Saturday. They follow that workout with another walk-through Sunday, then three straight full practices Monday through Wednesday.

title: Arizona Cardinals Training Camp Notebook: Day 7
full_text:
GLENDALE — It was a low and slow day for the Arizona Cardinals, as Thursday presented a jog-through for the team as they progress through the stages of training camp .
We're one week removed from their first preseason game, where Arizona will battle the Carolina Panthers in the NFL's Hall of Fame game.
It will be interesting to see how Arizona shifts their schedule with an actual game approaching, though Thursday was a scheduled low day for the team.
As such, we don't have much to report. The Cardinals had their typical suspects present during the open portion of practice.
However, we did talk to three key people. Here's the best thing each said:
Teryl Austin makes his return to the desert after previously serving as the Cardinals' defensive backs coach from 2007-09. Now, he's in a senior defensive coach position.
"It's been good, I gotta thank Mike [LaFleur] and Monti [Ossenfort] for it, because this role I'm doing is new. They just brought it up. They made it up because they thought I could help, and I got to thank them for giving me an opportunity to come in. And so it's been good. It was different getting back in the building. It's like the same building, but I don't remember my way around," Austin told reporters.
"... The bottom line is what's your job here? My job is to try to help us become a better football team, help the players develop as players and people and get them to reach their potential. Because if you do that stuff, then I think success follows."
Second-round pick Chase Bisontis has mostly been relegated to backup duties at right guard despite heavy expectations of him earning the starting job over Isaiah Adams.
Offensive line coach Justin Frye says Bisontis simply needs more time on task, which will come as we get deeper into camp and preseason play.
"It's just it's appearances at the plate, like you know baseball you see pitches, you get more acclimated to it. Football's the same," Frye said.
"Obviously, with Chase, you got the label of where they're picked. The anticipation, what they expect out of that, you've got to kind of block out all the noise with those guys, and he's done a great job with that."
Tyler Allgeier inked a two-year contract this offseason to tote the rock in Arizona, earning what was believed to be a bigger role compared to his previous stop in Atlanta. However, the Cardinals drafted Jeremiyah Love with the third overall pick, putting a massive damper on those hopes.
Allgeier gave his first words to reporters since Love was drafted:
"I felt like it was good. You know, the front office has their reasons and all of that, but I think it's just another weapon to get on the offensive side. I think it was a great pick. Great player. Great competition in the room, and we got, really a backed up room, so it's great to have. I think depth, especially in this league, is always great to have. Just having a lot of options [is big], so he's a great piece."
The Cardinals return to practice tomorrow (Friday, July 30) which begins at 1:45 PM.

title: Antonio Brown Tells Marvin Harrison Jr. to Make This 1 Change
full_text:
GLENDALE — Arizona Cardinals WR Marvin Harrison Jr. has made headlines as training camp is fully underway, but not for the best reasons.
Harrison, entering his third season, is looking to take a leap so many have been hoping for — and while the Cardinals' wideout has found himself open far more times than not, miscues and drops have been the narratives around Harrison thus far.
Harrison's gone viral for all the wrong reasons , though legendary receiver Antonio Brown offered a bit of advice online for Harrison:
"Take your shield off Marv," he put on X. "(eyes) to ball."
Take your shield off Marv  👀 s to ball 👃 🏈 https://t.co/olHVJnt5xh
Harrison typically sports a clear visor on his facemask, so Brown (who didn't during his career) believes that would be a step in the right direction. Some players wear it for eye protection while others believe it makes them look better.
It's also possible the lights of State Farm Stadium reflect just a bit awkwardly with the visor, especially when tracking deep balls.
But is it really just the visor?
There's some who believe Harrison's struggles stems from concentration in the transition to after the catch and/or simply his overall confidence.
Cardinals coach Mike LaFleur says sometimes mistakes happen, though Harrison bounced back the right way.
"What I was happy about Marvin and the one drop that you're alluding to is how he responded," he said.
"... All you tell these guys is, 'do the next right thing.' And the next right thing was to lineup, get back to the huddle, and the next opportunity you have — whether it's in the run game or the pass game — go full throttle and make it happen.
"And I thought the next time he had an opportunity to catch a football, he caught it, and we kept it moving right there. So we acknowledge it, and then we move on."
The Cardinals will need Harrison at his best this season, and there's hope a mixture of LaFleur's ability to scheme advantageous passing concepts mixed with Harrison's health and improvement will see his best season yet ahead of 2026.
Arizona certainly needs it if they're going to get LaFleur's tenure off on the right foot.
Harrison is a player that goes the extra mile in terms of physical and mental preparation ahead of the season. He's clearly shown the talent that made him the No. 4 overall pick years ago — he just needs to string it all together.

title: Surprise Playmaker Is Already Turning Heads at Cardinals Training Camp
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals are fully underway into their 2026 training camp session, and players are beginning to separate themselves from the pack.
We've seen typical big names such as Budda Baker and Trey McBride make plays, though summertime at State Farm Stadium is always good for a camp surprise or two.
This year, it's wide receiver Ihmir Smith-Marsette.
Smith-Marsette will turn 27 years old next month and is on his sixth NFL team. He is listed at 6-1 and 200 pounds on the Cardinals' official team site and played his college football at Iowa before being made a fifth-round pick in the 2021 NFL Draft.
Smith-Marsette initially began his career with the Minnesota Vikings before eventually making his way to the Chicago Bears, Kansas City Chiefs (where he won a Super Bowl), Carolina Panthers and most recently the New York Giants before landing in the desert this offseason.
Smith-Marsette is currently on a future/reserve contract.
Smith-Marsette is in a Cardinals receiver's room that features the likes of Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson and Kendrick Bourne, so opportunities to really make a splash will come few and far between.
However, Smith-Marsette is doing just that. His speed to create separation against defenders and ability to bring down catches either across the middle or deep down the sideline has been evident this training camp.
Ihmir Smith-Marsette is quietly having a really nice camp. I think he can make the 53. pic.twitter.com/WQLGQnwu87
The Cardinals don't have a bonafide "explosive" receiver in the mix. Harrison does many things at a high level while Wilson is their strongest contested catch artist and Bourne is a reliable slot receiver, though Arizona doesn't quite have a burner or deep threat.
Smith-Marsette possesses the acceleration to take a top off of opposing defenses, and he just might be one of the Cardinals' fastest wideouts.
While his ability as a receiver has been showcased, it's really another facet of his game that can see him sneak onto the 53-man roster.
Regardless if the Cardinals keep five or six receivers, Smith-Marsette's special teams value is going to either land him on the final roster after preseason cuts or at very minimum will generate some tough conversations in that process.
Smith-Marsette has consistently been in the group of return men on special teams while he's also a capable gunner. In his last two seasons played, Smith-Marsette logged 34% of special teams snaps played.
That's exactly how you earn a spot on an NFL team. When teams are identifying the final building blocks for their initial 53-man roster, special teams value and the ability to wear multiple hats on gameday can very much play into Smith-Marsette's favor.
He's a talented receiver. He's a willing special teams contributor. And he's been a surprise player turning heads at Cardinals training camp thus far.

title: Everything We Saw From Arizona Cardinals Training Camp: Day 6
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals are now fully a week into training camp.
Practice No. 6 just concluded at State Farm Stadium, and Carson Beck had perhaps one of his best performances of camp yet.
The third-round rookie has admittedly struggled through the early portions of summer ball, and even got off to a shaky start before flashing some of his arm talent during the final period of practice, which was a two-minute drill. Beck threaded two impressive throws during the drive, the last of which was lasering a ball between two defenders on a slant pattern for a touchdown.
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur on why Arizona doesn't do seven-on-seven drills:
"Seven on seven is not real football, and one on ones, you will see that today. I do like one on one O-line vs D-line play because you can at least put the five out there, and then the ball snapped ... To me, it's [seven-on-seven] fake ball and it's a unnecessary strain that has, to me, not a lot of value in terms of what actual football looks like."
The Cardinals have a "jog-through" on Thursday, which begins at noon. They'll have practice again on Friday before Saturday is a rest day.

title: Mike LaFleur Has Correct Mindset on Marvin Harrison Jr.'s Training Camp Drop
full_text:
GLENDALE — Marvin Harrison Jr. is the talk of the town, but not in a good way.
The Arizona Cardinals' third-year wideout went viral yesterday during the fifth day of training camp after dropping an open pass during practice.
Incomplete ball to Marv. Got open nicely but didn’t catch it. pic.twitter.com/fVJA0UDGuG
The drop has generated plenty of talk around Harrison and his potential role with the Cardinals moving into the future, though head coach Mike LaFleur isn't worried.
"You don't want to drop any balls ever, in the history of time. No receiver, tight end, running backs. Unfortunately, it does happen every once in a while," LaFleur told reporters.
"What I was happy about Marvin and the one drop that you're alluding to is how he responded. And the next time he had an opportunity, we have Trey [McBride] going underneath. We saw kind of an overlap underneath, Jacoby [Brissett] did, and he was able to layer one right over the middle to Marv. And all you tell these guys is, 'do the next right thing.' And the next right thing was to lineup, get back to the huddle, and the next opportunity you have — whether it's in the run game or the pass game — go full throttle and make it happen.
"And I thought the next time he had an opportunity to catch a football, he caught it, and you know we kept it moving right there. So we acknowledge it, and then we move on."
Harrison has played well during his third training camp, getting himself open often and coming down with nearly every target. However when it comes to the former No. 4 overall pick, fans online will be more critical than usual.
Harrison's known to be a bit harder on himself than the average person, whether by way of personality or the sheer expectations that followed him to the desert.
"He is a cerebral guy. The game makes sense to him, and so he is going to think about that stuff. That's a fair question, because I'm not even talking about Marv, I'm just talking in general over the time being with players," LaFleur said.
"Where is that fine line where it's obsessive and it locks you up, but also where it just gives you that edge? Each guy's a little bit different."
Harrison's teammates were quick to back the wideout, showing support immediately after and propping him up.
"Ultimately, it's a brotherhood. They spend a lot of time with each other. Marv's a good dude, like a lot of our guys," said LaFleur.
"And so our guys want to see other guys have success ... Hey, he had the drop, and then he responded with a big play, and ultimately had a bunch of explosives the other day."

title: The Truth Behind Cardinals' Viral Jeremiyah Love Quote
full_text:
GLENDALE — You've probably seen a viral quote making the rounds on Arizona Cardinals RB Jeremiyah Love and offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett's lack of excitement on the first-round pick.
Something along the lines of this:
Cardinals OC Nathaniel Hackett on Jeremiyah Love’s progression: “I mean, he’s definitely a rookie.” pic.twitter.com/cZ2Mkkt0YG
Welcome to 2026, where full quotes are left out for the sake of engagement and a single sentence can torch the overwhelming majority of people who didn't actually digest the full picture.
Hackett's full quote isn't a glowing endoresement of the No. 3 overall pick, but it does shed a brighter light compared to social media's iteration:
Hackett, entering the first year of his tenure in Arizona, has been vocal on rookies simply being the under-experienced players that they are. Such was the case when he talked about Carson Beck back in June:
"He is a rookie, and rookies — they're difficult at times. They come from a different system, a different world, a different speed."
Hackett has yet to singularly highlight one player during press conferences, adopting more of a strategy to speak on the entire room of a position group instead of propping up just one person.
Love has drawn rave reviews since entering the building in late April. Nothing has changed in that department.
In the early days of training camp, Love has earned multiple first-team reps during p. He's clearly going to have a role within Arizona's offense, and by the end of the season, it could be a prominent one.
However, the Cardinals were never going to deploy a bellcow approach to their backfield, and regardless of how good Love shows himself, players such as Tyler Allgeier and James Conner will still get their respective touches.
Hackett's role in the desert is also being overblown. The Cardinals' play-caller will be head coach Mike LaFleur, who also is gearing up to handle majority of the scheming. Not to say Hackett's opinion doesn't mean much for the Cardinals, but it's pretty clear who is running the show.
Case in point, people really need to stop reading too much into shortened quotes and taking things massively out of context.

title: Marvin Harrison Jr.'s Viral Drop Was a Reminder of His Biggest Question
full_text:
GLENDALE — Arizona Cardinals WR Marvin Harrison Jr . is one of the more polarizing players in the NFL.
That was already the case for the established fan base here in the desert, though a recent clip of Harrison dropping a pass (posted by yours truly) went viral during yesterday's practice . Everybody from Barstool to Sleeper to Underdog and so many other accounts posted it.
Incomplete ball to Marv. Got open nicely but didn’t catch it. pic.twitter.com/fVJA0UDGuG
The thousands of comments towards Harrison were only outmatched by the millions of views. It became apparent, instantly, Harrison is a player that will be judged by an immediate snap of a finger on any given day.
That's not exactly news for a professional football player, though some have it worse than others. In example, Ihmir Smith-Marsette dropped a crossing route last week and my mentions on X weren't flooded. Harrison drops a pass and the internet is set ablaze.
Yet there's a staunch difference between the two. Harrison was the fourth overall pick, was labeled a generational talent and carries a legendary last name. He's entering a pivotal third season after having not met lofty expectations thus far.
Fair or not, Harrison was expected to elevate Arizona's offense overnight the moment he was drafted. Reasons as to why are often debated, though the truth belongs somewhere in the middle of player vs. circumstance.
Drops are the buzzword when discussing Harrison, which have followed him from his very first NFL game, where his first target was a concentration drop. From there, there's been a few other moments where Harrison's been open but has failed to come down with a catch — most fans remember last season against San Francisco and his struggles against Seattle.
Yesterday's drop in camp didn't tell the whole story of Harrison's practice, or overall performance this summer.
He's consistently gotten open and has had far more catches than drops this training camp. He hasn't looked like the best wide receiver in the NFL, though he's also far from just being an average wideout. The tools and reasons why fans were so excited to land Harrison are still very much present, and with Mike LaFleur in town, there's hope Harrison will find himself more open than ever.
Yet the drop was also a reminder of what Harrison has been through his first two years in the league. You have to accept the good with the bad when it comes to No. 18 on the field, and thus far, Harrison's shown himself liable to mistakes on more than one occasion.
It's hard to ignore those, especially in the live circumstances they live in, though Harrison doesn't quite have a drop problem. His drop percentage (according to Pro Football Reference ) of 5.5% last season ranked No. 62 in the NFL and below receivers such as Amon-Ra St. Brown, in example.
Harrison works hard. Teammates and coaches rave about his work ethic and desire to be better from a mental and physical standpoint. The reason why so many were sold on Harrison being a no-brainer in the league was his elite college film paired with an impeccable work ethic.
When the two have married, Harrison's shown he can run with the best of them.
Yet many in the desert wonder if Harrison simply has a confidence problem. There's been a few times where he's gotten down on himself and openly discussed his battles with confidence in scrums/press conferences. Sometimes his body language is telling of that, too.
And last we forget, he's a young man about to turn 24 and has a different level of pressure compared to 99% of the population.
Yet Harrison's in a business where NFL stands for Not For Long , and the Cardinals have a massive decision approaching on his fifth-year option following the 2026 season.
LaFleur has consistently preached patience yet urgency when it comes to learning curves from his players, and if this coming campaign again fails to produce those coveted big results, even more doubt will hover over Harrison.
Yesterday's drop wasn't the end of the world. It shouldn't and won't define Harrison and what he can be this season for the Cardinals — because they are counting on him. However, it was a reminder that perhaps the Ohio State product still has some people to prove wrong.
And they'll need to see it before they believe it.

title: Cardinals Camp Notebook, Day 5: Pads On, Physicality Up
full_text:
GLENDALE — Lights. Camera. Action.
The pads came on for the first time today at State Farm Stadium as the Cardinals now progress into the second phase of training camp.
There's a different sense of physicality when the pads come on as the rushing attack is able to gain a better and more realistic feel as opposed to the initial days of camp - where Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur dubbed it a "passing camp" to begin festivities.
A recap from a busy (and brusing) day in the desert:
Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur on ramping up the physicality up with pads:
"There's going to be collisions out there, obviously, and when the ball carrier is going, particularly between the tackles, and there's opportunities to thud up frontal, they'll do that. And then they'll let them go, and then the shots will come.
"I told the guys if anyone in the hole has a shot to thud them up, thud them up. I don't want to see 11 guys thudding up. That's not realistic. So let them go, and then go get your shot on the ball so that you're 1: you're training yourself and 2: you're training the [running] backs. If it's out in open space or a ball's thrown over the middle, those guys got to be pros. I mean, they're the elite of the elite out there, and guys got to know how to practice.
"Typically the guys that don't know how to practice are the guys that just can't stick around because they're not capable of it. I look forward to seeing them be physical but being smart at the same time."
The Cardinals are back in action tomorrow on Wednesday, July 29, with practice beginning at 4:00 PM.

title: Marvin Harrison Jr. Injury Update Gives Cardinals Fans Sigh of Relief
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals saw star receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. deal with multiple injuries during their last training camp practice, which raised some concerns over his health.
After the team had a scheduled day off on Monday, the Cardinals are back to work, and it appears Harrison should be just fine.
"Cramping. Yep. He's totally good. He was cramping," Cardinals head coach Mike LaFleur said of Harrison ahead of Tuesday's practice, where pads are set to come on for the first time.
Harrison initially was spotted hobbling early in Sunday's practice before later landing awkwardly on his side.
Marvin Harrison Jr. has been in some obvious discomfort since coming down with a sideline catch during team drills. Cards have tomorrow off before returning to action on Tuesday. pic.twitter.com/mXbDseFWGc
Harrison's entering a critical third season in the league after his initial stint in Arizona has seen highs and lows. The No. 4 overall pick, once labeled generational, now faces a massive season where there's hope LaFleur can maximize his talents.
In a crowded Cardinals pass-catchers room that also features Trey McBride and Michael Wilson, Harrison will have ample opportunity to establish himself – though there won't be a defined WR1 in Arizona.
"You just try to put them in those positions. Who [receiver] one is number one on the progression for that play. And you're trying to do that balancing act of like, hey, we got talent. Don't overthink this thing. Don't try to get too schemy. Let these guys go out and play fast [and] do what they do well," LaFleur said.
"But at the same time, [we need to] put them in positions where you know it's not a dead play, if you will. So there's a lot of lot of elements to it.
"There's so much to it in terms of putting these guys in positions that we think they're going to be successful within the scheme that we're trying to get done and the defense that we're going against."
Harrison is coming off a season where he suffered from appendicitis, two heel injuries and a concussion — causing him to miss five games. He told reporters he still wasn't 100% healthy back in June when mandatory minicamp was rolling.
"I go 100% [during practice]. I'm still out there doing everything I normally would do, but yeah, it's just like an ongoing process for sure," Harrison said.
The Cardinals are entering their fifth practice of 2026's training camp period. Their first preseason action will come on Thursday, Aug. 6 in the NFL's Hall of Fame Game against the Carolina Panthers.

title: Jeremiyah Love Is Already Turning Heads at Arizona Cardinals Camp
full_text:
ARIZONA — $50 million can get you far in life. Oftentimes, no amount of money can buy love, but for the Arizona Cardinals, they've been nothing short of heart eyes over their star rookie.
Rookie running back Jeremiyah Love has very much looked the part of a playmaker through the early stages of his Cardinals tenure. It's tough for running backs to really establish themselves in training camp — without pads — but Love's been able to do just that.
“Obviously, I haven’t met with Jeremiyah yet,” Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett said. “But being able to be here and watch him practice and do his thing — I see why we paid him $50 million."
I would not have a linebacker in coverage on Jeremiyah Love pic.twitter.com/h33HLQTqkF
Love, the third overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, has earned every bit of praise since first stepping foot in the team's facility. The way he carries himself off the field in terms of maturity and leadership has only been countered by the lighting-quick agility and vision he's displayed early on at State Farm Stadium.
A three-win team drafting a running back that high typically is laughed at — and the Cardinals surely were on the end of online backlash from media and fans alike following the pick. Rarely does a player at a devalued position truly make a difference, though Arizona believes Love is a rare weapon capable of doing damage as both a runner and pass-catcher.
Jeremiyah Love’s initial burst is just different man. pic.twitter.com/VCk5D51Qtf
ESPN's Matt Bowen ranked Love's pick 12th out of the most impactful moves made this offseason across the entire league:
"Love should be viewed as a three-down playmaker, similar to how Jahmyr Gibbs was seen as a rookie with the Lions. Love scored 21 total touchdowns for Notre Dame in 2025, and he was a home run hitter with 39 rushes of 10 or more yards. Plus, Love had 63 receptions during his college career, and his route tree should expand in the Cardinals' offense."
Love doesn't project as a bellcow back. That's not what head coach Mike LaFleur has deployed previously at other stops and that's not likely to change with Tyler Allgeier and James Conner firmly in the mix.
He also won't be a savior of the franchise. That's far too heavy of a weight for any rookie to carry, let alone a running back.
However, he's been everything as advertised through the early stages of camp, and that should continue as the pads come on today.

title: Atlanta Falcons Reunite With Former Player, Cut Former Second-Round Pick
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons added important special-teams depth by reuniting with former linebacker Josh Woods, according to a team press release on Thursday morning. The Falcons released defensive lineman Ross Blacklock in a corresponding move.
Woods, who played for the Falcons in 2024 and 2025, was not re-signed by the new regime during the offseason. They opted to let him test free agency, but the veteran linebacker went unsigned during that period.
The defender from Maryland originally joined the Chicago Bears as an undrafted free agent following the 2018 NFL Draft. Over his seven seasons in the league, Woods has spent time with Chicago (2019-21), Detroit Lions (2020-22), Arizona Cardinals (2023) and the Atlanta Falcons (2024-25). He has appeared in 82 games, making eight starts and registering 137 tackles (85 solo), four tackles for loss, three quarterback hits, 0.5 sacks, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery, and one pass defense.
The majority of his work has come on special teams, but he will have the opportunity to provide some necessary depth at linebacker, too. The Falcons have Divine Deablo and Christian Harris splitting reps with the first unit, but there is plenty of competition behind those two.
Rookies Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins Jr. were added in the spring, but so was veteran Channing Tindall. Those three are competing with returning players JD Bertrand, Malik Verdon, and the still-injured Troy Andersen. That room remains in flux, but there will be plenty of competition to follow along with this summer.
Blacklock, a former second-round pick the Falcons signed back in May , has been in the league since 2020, but the 27-year-old has bounced around the league since then. He has made stops on active rosters with the Texans (2020-21), Vikings (2022), Jaguars (2023), and Titans (2023). He also signed on with the Colts (2023) and Giants (2024) as part of their practice squads, but he was unsigned in 2025.
The defensive lineman from TCU has played in 44 career games, making three starts, but none since 2023. Over that time, he has picked up 40 tackles, five tackles for loss, 3.0 sacks, and a forced fumble. Now, he will be looking for a new team again after failing to stick with the Falcons as the team opts to reunite with a former contributor.

title: Falcons Camp Preview: Breaking Down an Overhauled Wide Receiver Room
full_text:
Seven receptions, 42 yards. Outside of Drake London, that is the only returning production to the Atlanta Falcons ' wide receiver room for the 2026 season.
The position saw the biggest changes from last season to this one. The changes were needed after the position group garnered just 892 yards outside of London last season. The Falcons were in desperate need of an overhaul at the position. So what does the room look like now, and what should Falcons fans expect?
Drake London returns to the Falcons' wide receiver room with a new contract under his belt . After being the only dependable wide receiver target last season and promising production in his first four years in the league, London earned himself a massive payday.
In just 12 games last season, London hauled in 68 catches for 919 yards and seven touchdowns. His big frame combined with his strong hands gives him excellent contested catch skills. He is also a fluid route runner for his size, which makes him a tough matchup for any corner.
London will once again be the Falcons' primary wide receiver and will mostly feature as the X, or outside receiver, but will also be moved inside to slot on occasion, where he has seen success in the past.
The only other returning receiver who caught a pass for the Falcons last season is Dylan Drummond. Drummond caught seven of his 11 targets for 42 yards. At 6-foot-0, 190 pounds, Drummond has an average receiver build and, because of this, can play either of the outside receiver positions. If he makes the team again in 2026 , he will serve as a depth piece for the Falcons' receiver room once again in 2026.
Chris Blair will be returning for his fourth season with the Falcons as well. Blair has caught only one pass for 17 yards in his three seasons with the team, but has remained a practice squad player that the team likes to call on when injuries occur.
The Falcons added three main pieces to the receiver room to help bolster the position for the 2026 season. Each of these three has their own unique skill sets that complement London’s and make for a well-rounded receiver room.
The first of those names is Jahan Dotson. The Falcons signed Dotson to a two-year, $15 million contract in the offseason. He had previously played with the Philadelphia Eagles, where the former first-round pick struggled for targets in an offense that ran the ball at a high rate and had two elite wide receivers taking the bulk of the targets.
Still, Dotson put up back-to-back 500-yard seasons during his first two years in the league with the Washington Commanders before winning a Super Bowl with the Eagles in his two years there.
He now joins the Falcons, where his elite speed and good ball tracking skills will slot him into the starting Z receiver opposite Drake London on the outside. Dotson’s skill set will give the Falcons a deep-threat receiver that they were missing out on last season.
The Falcons also used a third-round pick to select University of Georgia receiver Zachariah Branch . Branch was a five-star recruit out of high school and played his first two years at USC before joining the Bulldogs.
Branch possesses great speed and elite twitch. He is not the biggest target, standing at 5-foot-10, 180 pounds, but his speed and elusiveness make him extremely dangerous with the ball in his hands. He has also shown some promise as another deep ball threat early in offseason workouts.
His big-play ability should help him find the field early as the Falcons' slot receiver and gadget guy. He will also most likely be featured as a returner throughout the year, a role he excelled in during his time in college.
The final major addition the Falcons made to the room was bringing back Olamide Zaccheaus, who played for the team from 2019-2022. The seven-year pro brings veteran leadership and stability to the position.
His route-running ability and consistent hands will have him splitting reps with Branch at the slot receiver position. A solid veteran piece was a welcome addition to a receiver group full of young and talented players.
The Falcons signed three undrafted free agents to compete for spots on the team, including Vinny Anthony II, Le’Meke Brockington, and Keelan Marion. Marion is the most likely to earn a roster spot. He finished his final year at the University of Miami with 57 catches for 746 yards and two touchdowns while also excelling as a kick returner.
The Falcons also signed second-year player Antwane Wells Jr., who was on the Giants' practice squad for parts of last year.
With the starting jobs mostly decided, these players will compete in training camp for the backup spots. They are all unproven, so it is difficult to judge the room's depth with almost no experience to draw on, but that also means there is upside. After the bar was set so low last season, this is an area ripe for improvement in 2026.

title: Falcons Training Camp Day 2: Bijan Robinson Watch has Officially Begun
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons hit the field on Thursday morning for their second day of training camp under new head coach Kevin Stefanski.
Yesterday's news was dominated by the players who were or were not participating, including running back Bijan Robinson and quarterbacks Michael Penix Jr. and Tua Tagovailoa.
The same could be said for Thursdays practice as there was more shuffling, players limited in their participation, and another key sideline spectator.
There was rampant speculation this spring that the Atlanta Falcons would get a contract extension done for star running back Bijan Robinson, despite the fact that he has two years remaining on his rookie deal. After sitting out his second day of training camp, it's hard to characterize his position as anything other than a hold-in (he's fined heavily if he doesn't show up at all in a hold-out).
Robinson is scheduled to earn a base salary of $1.1 million and a roster bonus of $2.6 million. He was paid a $13 million signing bonus as a rookie, bringing his cap number to $7 million for the season.
Robinson's new contract will likely pay him in the neighborhood of $25 million annually. That's roughly 28 cents on the dollar if you're Robinson or his agent, for a position with a notoriously short shelf life.
From the Falcons' point of view, they have him under a guaranteed contract for two more seasons, and financially speaking, it makes a lot more sense to wait at least a year to get an extension done. We've seen running backs fall off a cliff from a production standpoint as they enter their second contracts.
But Robinson is the face of the Falcons right now, their best player, and coming off an All-Pro season. The Falcons want to get a new deal done for Robinson, and it makes sense that it will get done in the coming days. If I'm his agent, I tell him, "Bijan, we're almost done; don't go back out there and get hurt until we are done."
However, that's speculation. Until we hear something new, the Bijan Robinson watch has officially begun.
Tua Tagovailoa missed day one of training camp entirely, but he was back on the field on Thursday morning. He was limited in what they let him do. He threw some balls, but didn't take part in any footwork, 7v7s, or 11v11 team drills.
Penix was late to the field, leading to speculation that it could be a scheduled rest day after he carried a heavy load on Wednesday. Despite not being cleared for 11v11s, he took the majority of the reps in every other aspect of practice and looked sharp.
With both potential starting quarterbacks missing snaps, undrafted free agent Jack Strand took the majority of the reps, followed by newly signed Cooper Rush. Strand made some good throws and showed some mobility.
Every day that goes by, it's harder and harder not to see Strand making the 53-man roster .
Atlanta made a roster move ahead of practice, waiving defensive tackle Ross Blacklock and signing linebacker Josh Woods. Both players have played the roster shuffle over the course of the last year, and we'll probably see their names on transaction reports again before too long.
2nd-year offensive tackle Jack Nelson was inside on the exercise bike after running with the second team on Wednesday.
The nickel position looks like one of the most unsettled (outside of quarterback) at camp. Sydney Brown came out with the ones during 11v11s. A.J. Woods saw rotation with the first team and the third team, and rookie Avieon Terrell worked in and made an excellent pass breakup during team drills.
Strand made a nice pass on the goal line to Drake London. London used his body against Terrell to make a contested catch. It was called short of a touchdown, and he angrily kicked the ball away.
In a running play, edge rusher Bralen Trice did an excellent job of sealing the edge and forcing the running back inside. He finished off the play by making the tackle. He's bigger than anyone else in the edge room and did an excellent job of showing a role he can carve out for himself.
Chris Blair had the catch of the day on a diving out route for a touchdown. Blair is trying to make the back end of the roster, and he helped his cause on Thursday.
James Pearce Jr. was still working with the third team today, and he made it awfully difficult for the third team offense to run plays. As he works his way back into shape, he'll move back up the depth chart.
Team president Matt Ryan helped warm up the wide receivers with some sharp passing. No, he's not coming back.
Well, you might recognize the QB throwing routes for the shorthanded Falcons. pic.twitter.com/PHQO2Kc5fx
The Falcons will be back on the field on Friday morning as season ticket holders will also be in attendance before practice opens for fans on Saturday.
